rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture all 10 compounds and reveal the retention range and critical separations. The high final organic fraction and remaining hold time help expose strongly retained components.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin survives. Keep composition endpoints and temperature fixed to isolate the gradient-slope effect.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover separation in the crowded middle region while targeting a last-peak time below 10 minutes. This tests whether gradient slope alone can deliver full resolution without a time penalty.

Raise temperature by 5 °C to test whether selectivity improves for the remaining critical pair while keeping the promising 14-minute gradient. The current last-peak time leaves some margin to achieve full resolution without a time penalty.

The temperature shift suggests the critical pair is approaching an elution-order crossover; moving to 55 °C tests whether separation reopens beyond it. Higher temperature should also keep the last peak below the time-penalty threshold.

Slightly steepen the gradient at 55 °C to try to lift the remaining critical separation above 1.5 while preserving the neighboring pair’s resolution margin. The shorter gradient should keep the time penalty at zero.

Slightly increase the gradient slope to test whether the critical pair gains resolution while retaining the maximum CRF. The neighboring pair has some resolution margin, and the last peak should elute slightly earlier.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, test a higher-temperature, shallower-gradient alternative for a larger resolution margin. The shallower gradient may protect the neighboring separation as temperature further separates the current critical pair.

Test starting organic fraction as an additional selectivity lever at the successful 55 °C temperature. This slightly shallower gradient may improve the neighboring separation while the higher starting organic fraction limits retention time.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek more resolution margin while retaining CRF 1.000. Injection 9 suggests this direction may improve the critical pair, and its last-peak time leaves room for a modest increase.

Slightly flatten injection 10’s gradient to recover the neighboring pair’s resolution from 1.41 to at least 1.5. The other critical pair has some margin at 1.74, and the last peak should remain below the time-penalty threshold.

Further flatten the gradient slightly to balance the two closest separations and seek a larger minimum-resolution margin. Based on injection 11, the last peak should still elute below 10 minutes, preserving the opportunity for CRF 1.000.

The maximum CRF is already secured; explore a lower-temperature selectivity regime for an alternative fully resolved method. The 12-minute gradient should offset increased retention while testing whether critical separations reopen after elution-order changes.

Return to the successful 55 °C regime and slightly flatten injection 9’s gradient to test a nearby method with full resolution. This should preserve a zero time penalty while mapping the operating range that achieves CRF 1.000.

Test whether a much steeper gradient at 60 °C carries the crowded middle peaks through an elution-order crossover and restores full separation. The maximum CRF is already secured; this explores a substantially faster alternative.

Shorten the gradient further to test whether the close pair at 60 °C separates after its apparent elution-order crossover. This explores a faster alternative while retaining the previously established CRF 1.000 methods as the campaign best.

Return to the fully resolved region using a gradient slope close to injection 12, with a higher final organic fraction. This should retain its improved resolution margin and zero time penalty while testing another method capable of the maximum CRF.
Use a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 to seek a shorter method that retains full resolution. Its two closest separations should remain near or above 1.5, with no expected time penalty.
Slightly steepen injection 18’s gradient to test a faster alternative that may retain CRF 1.000. The observed resolution margins suggest both critical separations could remain above 1.5.

Extend the higher-starting-organic, shallower-gradient direction to test whether it offers greater resolution margin while preserving CRF 1.000. Monitor both the earliest peaks and the middle critical pairs, since increased starting organic may compress those separations.

Return to the successful 0.15 starting fraction with a gradient slope between injections 11 and 17. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty while testing a lower final organic fraction and shorter programmed gradient.

Use nearly the same gradient slope as injection 17, which achieved CRF 1.000 with a minimum resolution of 1.70, but terminate the gradient earlier. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction preserves complete elution and the maximum score.

Match injection 7’s successful gradient slope while lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient. Because its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this gradient would end at the outlet, this method should preserve full resolution and CRF 1.000.

Match injection 12’s gradient slope but transition to the final hold earlier, testing a lower-organic endpoint. The critical separations should be preserved; the main uncertainty is whether the last peak still elutes before the time penalty begins.

Use the final injection to test temperature sensitivity around injection 22’s fully resolved method. The campaign has already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000; this run assesses whether that performance extends to 50 °C.
